name: Thulung
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Allen, N. J. 1975. Sketch of Thulung Grammar, with three texts and a glossary. Cornell East Asia Series 6. Ithaca, NY: Cornell University China-Japan Program (online edition 2007, Cornell eCommons handle 1813/57638).
catalog_locator: Ch. II (Phonology), sec. 5 'Notes on word stress', pp. 37-38; vocative remark ch. IV sec. 1.2 'Vocatives', p. 96
catalog_quote: 5. Notes on word stress. Only some miscellaneous observations can be offered. Syllabic stress probably never has phonemic status in isolation from length. Most words have, if anything, only a weak stress on the first syllable. In the following three groups of exceptions the stressed syllable is often long drawn out and of higher pitch. It is indicated with an acute accent. 5.1. Certain reduplicates. griŋgríŋya "welling up copiously" om-ómya "yellowish" toaptoápwa "each to his own" kokó dep "here and there" hahám huhúm "a few scraps" 5.2. Some expressions of quantity and direction. katíkoloŋ "just a little" (ali ali N) contrasts with katikoloŋ "some, a bit" (alikati N). aketí kelpa "as small as this" (yeti sāno N) contrasts with akoti kolpa "of such and such a size" (yetro N). Here the stress and pitch phenomenon is accompanied by an uncommon change in quality of the neighbouring vowels, cf. IV 2.34 and V 1.34). halá hatla "up there" 5.3. Vocatives. wa-á "elder sibling" (vocative of wa) dewá nokchó "priest" (vocative of dewa nokcho) 5.4. recha The borrowed verbal auxiliary rahecha N is very common in Thulung in the form rechá. Its first syllable is often extremely brief.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is weak and non-phonemic (never contrastive independently of vowel length); where present it falls on the first syllable of the word. A small set of lexical exceptions (certain reduplicated expressives, a few quantity/direction expressions, vocative forms) carry a non-initial prominent syllable that is lengthened and higher in pitch, and this can be quasi-contrastive (katíkoloŋ 'just a little' vs katikoloŋ 'some').
new_statements.exceptions: Three groups: (5.1) certain reduplicates (e.g. griŋgríŋya 'welling up copiously', om-ómya 'yellowish', kokó dep 'here and there'); (5.2) some expressions of quantity and direction (katíkoloŋ vs katikoloŋ; aketí kelpa vs akoti kolpa; halá hatla 'up there'), where stress/pitch is accompanied by vowel-quality change; (5.3) vocatives (wa-á, dewá nokchó); (5.4) the Nepali loan auxiliary recha with an extremely brief first syllable. Elsewhere (ch. IV 1.2) the vocative 'may be expressed simply by additional stress and raised pitch on the final syllable'. Allen also reports a tentative tense/lax 'tone' contrast in a minority of words (ch. II 4, pp. 32-37), which Lahaussois (2002, 2004) could no longer find.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on words elicited in isolation by an anthropologist-fieldworker (1969-71, Mukli village); author flags the observations as miscellaneous and tentative. Lahaussois's later descriptions (2002 thesis, 2004 sketch) are silent on stress and report no tone.
new_statements.identity_note: Allen 1975 describes the Thulung of Mukli village (Solukhumbu, eastern Nepal), the same variety Lahaussois later worked on; no distinct dialect glottocode. Glottolog conflates Lahaussois's 2002 Berkeley thesis with a Pacific Linguistics volume in ref 50827; the file held by the project is the UC Berkeley dissertation from eScholarship. Glottolog ref 70258 (Lahaussois 'Thulung Rai', 2003) is the Himalayan Linguistics Archive 1 sketch dated 2004 on eScholarship.

tone_statements.quote: I mention below some of the features that intrigued—even astonished—me. 1. Vowel length is contrastive in verbs, but other parts of speech use it only sporadically or even allow free variation (p. 22). 2. Tone, though it proved too elusive for Allen to mark it regularly, is none the less used consistently to distinguish present and past tense in certain verbs (p. 33).

II sec. 5 'Notes on word stress' (pp. 37-38): stress probably never phonemic apart from length; most words have at most a weak stress on the first syllable; three exception groups (certain reduplicates, some quantity/direction expressions, vocatives) where the stressed syllable is drawn out and higher-pitched, marked with an acute accent. Ch. II sec. 4 (pp. 32-37) describes a tentative tense/lax 'tone' contrast in a minority of words. Vocative also expressed by extra stress and raised pitch on the final syllable (ch. IV 1.2, p. 105 area).

sources.note: Ch. 1 Phonology (pp. 33-52: syllable structure, initials, vowels, finals, rhymes, vowel length, tone p. 46, morphophonological rules). The words 'stress' and 'accent' occur nowhere in the text; silent on word stress. On tone (intro p. 18): 'I have not found any evidence of tone in Thulung', attributing Allen's tense/lax contrast to a system lost under Nepali contact. Vowel length said to be no longer phonemic except 'intonationally' for emphasis.
